title: Concerning a Civil Principality
hook: The loaf scale belongs in public; the private price slate belongs away from the crowd.
counterintuition: The mistake is to count who likes the new ruler. The better move is to ask who raised him, what that side wants, whether the people are protected from oppression, and which promises will survive adversity.
tryThisNow: Pick one leader raised by internal factions. Write who elevated them, what that group wants, how the people are protected, and what adversity would test first.
keyTakeaway: A civil prince is safer when his foundation protects the people from oppression, manages nobles as dangerous rivals, and keeps citizens needing the state in adversity.

breakdown.fastRead: A grain magistrate moves the mill owners' private price slate away from the public loaf scale. The mill owners want freedom to squeeze. The crowd wants bread not to be taken from them. That is the civil principality problem in miniature. A ruler raised inside the city must know whether nobles or people lifted him. The people can usually be satisfied by protection; nobles often want permission. Quiet-time promises are not adversity loyalty.
breakdown.deepRead:
A civil principality begins inside the city, not from foreign conquest, hereditary custom, or wicked seizure. A leading citizen becomes prince through the favour of the people or the favour of the nobles. That origin matters because the two sides want different things. Nobles want to command and oppress. The people mainly want not to be oppressed.

A harbor pilot stands over a velvet berth book while crews wait under a chalked tide board. Shipowners offer her the protector's office if she lets them control every berth. The fishers and deck crews raised her because they feared being squeezed out. If she rewards the shipowners first, she owes power to men who see themselves as her equals and expect room to dominate. If she writes crew appeal hours on the tide board, she builds on the side whose demand can be satisfied without making rivals stronger.

Nobles are fewer, but they are sharper dangers. They can conspire, bargain with the expected winner, or treat the prince as one of their own raised for their use. Some nobles bind themselves to his fortune and are worth honoring if they are not rapacious. Some hang back from timidity and can be used for counsel. Ambitious nobles who keep a second door open should be feared like enemies.

The people are many, and a hostile people cannot be secured against in the same way. Their demand is also easier to satisfy: do not oppress them. A prince built on the people is not standing on mud if he can command when danger arrives. The mud warning fits a private citizen who only hopes the people will rescue him; it does not fit a prince with authority, courage, and popular need behind him.
breakdown.fullRead:
A silver baton rests across extra levy tablets in a hill-town square. The noble houses have made a militia captain ruler during a peasant tax revolt. They expect him to use the baton as their instrument. Villagers expect punishment. If he keeps the baton and leaves the tablets intact, his title belongs to nobles who want to squeeze the town. If he breaks the levy tablets and has the protection decree read aloud, the people receive good where they expected harm.

Civil power has a distinct origin. A prominent citizen receives rule through internal favour, either from nobles or from the people. The city is pulled by two desires. Nobles want command and room to press everyone below them. The people do not want to be ruled and oppressed by them. Out of that tension can come principality, self-government, or disorder. The new prince has to read which side made him and what price that side expects.

A prince raised by nobles starts with difficulty because nobles near him often think they are his equals. They do not merely ask for safety. They ask for command, offices, exemptions, and room to press the people. Fair dealing cannot satisfy that appetite without injuring others. A prince raised by the people stands more alone, with fewer equals around him, and the people's request is narrower: protect us from oppression.

That does not make popular favour a slogan or a moral shortcut. The people can abandon a ruler if he cannot command, if he panics, or if old magistrates remain the channel of action in tumults. Popular foundations work only when the prince has authority and courage, keeps people encouraged, and makes them need the state and him in every condition. Promises made in calm weather do not prove who will move in danger.

A market-city judge shows the noble problem in a cooler form. Pledge tokens sit between two boards under an unlit siege lantern. In prosperity every noble promises support. Before a siege, the judge sorts each token: bound to our danger, or keeping another exit ready. The first kind may receive honor and command keys. The timid but wise can give counsel without being feared. The ambitious noble who avoids binding himself is preparing to save himself with whoever wins.

Nabis of Sparta is the pressure test. He faced all Greece and a victorious Roman army. Against such danger, securing himself against a few powerful men would not have been enough if the people were hostile. A few nobles can be watched, replaced, or deprived of authority. A hostile people are too many. The worst from the people is abandonment; from nobles can come abandonment plus active attack.

The magistrate problem adds another risk. A civil prince may rule through magistrates, and in quiet times that can look stable because citizens need the state and everyone promises loyalty. In tumults, citizens used to receiving orders from magistrates may wait for those old channels instead of obeying the prince directly. The experiment can only be tried once, because a flood, siege, or revolt will not pause while authority finds its voice.

That is why the river city matters. The prince calls from the balcony for sand crews, but people wait for the magistrates' drum before moving. Their applause in the square did not transfer command. If the old channel still carries obedience, direct rule exists on paper and fails in water.

Carry the rule carefully. Do not ask whether the ruler is popular in the easy sense. Ask who raised him, what they want, whether satisfying them would injure others, which nobles share his danger, and whether the people need him when danger comes. Popular protection can become a foundation when citizens depend on the state and move when the prince commands in adversity.

examples.title: Danel Moves the Price Slate

planSpec.domain: a grain-market magistrate elevated after mill owners and bakers clash over famine prices
planSpec.audience: a leading citizen deciding whether to owe office to mill owners or to market crowds
planSpec.stakes: mill owners want freedom to squeeze, while the crowd wants bread not to be taken from them; one demand can be satisfied without empowering equals
planSpec.requiredBeat: He moves the mill owners' private price slate away from the public loaf scale and posts the anti-seizure order where the crowd can see it.

examples.scenario: A public loaf scale stands beside a private mill owners' price slate in the grain market at 6:30 a.m. Danel, newly raised as magistrate after bakers and mill owners nearly fought over famine prices, must decide who his office answers to. He moves the private slate away from the scale and posts the anti-seizure order where the crowd can read it before bread is weighed.
examples.whatToDo: Make the first order protect the crowd from being squeezed. Danel should remove the private slate from public authority and post the anti-seizure rule visibly.
examples.whyItMatters: Mill owners want room to command prices. The crowd asks not to have bread taken from them, a demand the magistrate can satisfy without creating equal rivals.

examples.title: Meret Refuses the Velvet Book

planSpec.domain: a harbor pilot elected protector after shipowners try to control all berth assignments
planSpec.audience: a civic leader who rose because crews and fishers feared being squeezed by shipowners
planSpec.stakes: shipowners can conspire with money and captains, while ordinary crews only ask not to lose berths and wages
planSpec.requiredBeat: She refuses the shipowners' velvet berth register, writes crew appeal hours on a tide board, and makes the first order protect access rather than reward the men who offered her office.

examples.scenario: A velvet berth register lies closed beside a chalked tide board in the harbor office at 4:55 a.m. Meret, the pilot elected protector after shipowners tried to control every berth, must decide whether to accept the register they offer her. She refuses it, writes crew appeal hours on the tide board, and makes her first order protect access instead of rewarding the men who tried to buy her office.
examples.whatToDo: Protect berth access before honoring shipowners. Meret should put appeal hours in public view and refuse a private register that lets wealthy captains dominate the harbor.
examples.whyItMatters: Shipowners can conspire through money and captains. Crews and fishers ask for protection from exclusion, which gives the ruler a safer foundation.

examples.title: Orfeo Breaks the Levy Tablets

planSpec.domain: a hill-town militia captain made ruler by noble houses during a peasant tax revolt
planSpec.audience: a captain who owes his title to nobles but must win the people before adversity
planSpec.stakes: the noble houses see him as their equal and instrument, while villagers expected punishment and can become devoted if protected from extra levies
planSpec.requiredBeat: After accepting the nobles' silver baton, he breaks the extra levy tablets in the square and orders the tax clerks to read the protection decree aloud.

examples.scenario: A silver baton rests across extra levy tablets in Belvar's hill-town square outside the east tax hall at 12:05 p.m. Orfeo, the militia captain made ruler by noble houses, must decide how to answer villagers who expected punishment after the peasant tax revolt. He accepts the baton, then breaks the extra levy tablets in public and orders the tax clerks to read the protection decree aloud.
examples.whatToDo: Turn a noble-made title toward popular protection. Orfeo should keep the baton only while destroying the extra levy and making the protection decree public.
examples.whyItMatters: The nobles see him as their instrument. Protecting villagers from added levies gives him a foundation beyond the houses that raised him.

examples.title: Sabine Sorts the Pledge Tokens

planSpec.domain: a market-city judge studying which noble allies bind themselves to his fortune before a siege scare
planSpec.audience: a prince sorting nobles who are loyal, timid, useful for counsel, or ambitious enemies
planSpec.stakes: in prosperity all nobles promise support; in adversity, ambitious ones will save themselves by opening talks with the expected winner
planSpec.requiredBeat: The judge places each noble's pledge token on one of two boards: bound to our danger or keeping a second door open, then changes who receives command keys.

examples.scenario: Pledge tokens sit between two boards under an unlit siege lantern in the market court at 11:20 p.m. Sabine, the judge-prince, reviews the scare after the enemy withdraws. She places each noble's token on one board: bound to our danger, or keeping a second door open. Then she changes who receives command keys before the next alarm.
examples.whatToDo: Sort noble allies by adversity behavior. Sabine should honor those bound to her danger, use timid counselors carefully, and keep command keys from ambitious nobles with a second door.
examples.whyItMatters: In prosperity every noble can promise support. A siege scare reveals who shares the ruler's fortune and who is preparing to bargain with the expected winner.

examples.title: Caspar Hears the Drum Move Them

planSpec.domain: a river city transitioning from magistrate rule to direct command during flood defense
planSpec.audience: a civil prince learning that people used to magistrate orders may not obey him in tumults
planSpec.stakes: quiet-time applause means little if flood crews still look to magistrates while the embankment fails
planSpec.requiredBeat: He calls for sand crews from the balcony, then sees everyone wait for the magistrates' drum before moving, proving his authority has not passed through the old channel.

examples.scenario: A magistrates' drum hangs above stacked flood sand sacks in the river hall at 2:15 a.m. Caspar, newly direct ruler of the city, must decide whether balcony command has replaced old magistrate orders. He predicts his call will move crews to the embankment. He calls from above the square. No one moves until the magistrates' drum sounds.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the drum as the real command channel. Caspar should not trust quiet applause until flood crews move on his order without waiting for magistrates.
examples.whyItMatters: Citizens used to magistrate orders may freeze in tumults. Direct command exists only when people obey the prince at the moment the state needs them.

examples.title: Linnea Keeps the Rod on the Table

planSpec.domain: a textile city where guild workers raised a dyer to block merchant-house domination
planSpec.audience: a new civil prince deciding whether to keep the people needing the state and him
planSpec.stakes: workers can abandon him in adversity unless the dye-house courts, wage measures, and guard rotations make protection a daily dependence
planSpec.requiredBeat: When the merchant houses offer a banquet seat, he keeps his stained measuring rod on the wage court table and asks which order prevents oppression tomorrow morning.

examples.scenario: A stained measuring rod lies across a wage court table in the dyers' hall at 7:45 p.m. Linnea, the dyer raised by guild workers, must decide whether to take a merchant-house banquet seat or keep daily protection first. "They offer you a place tonight," a clerk says. A guard rotation slip waits beside the rod. "Which order prevents oppression tomorrow morning?" Linnea asks.
examples.whatToDo: Keep protection in daily instruments. Linnea should use wage courts, measuring rules, and guard rotations before accepting honors from merchant houses.
examples.whyItMatters: Workers raised her to block domination, but they can abandon her in adversity. Daily protection makes them need the state and ruler, not just admire them.

questions.prompt: A leading citizen becomes ruler after mill owners and market crowds clash over famine bread. No foreign army enters, and no hereditary claim is used. What kind of rule is this?
choices: A civil principality formed through internal favour.
A mixed principality gained by conquest.
A hereditary state protected by old custom.
questions.explanation: The ruler rises inside the city through citizens, not through conquest or inheritance. The next question is which internal side lifted him and what it wants.

questions.prompt: Shipowners offer a harbor protector private control of berth assignments. Crews ask only for appeal hours so they cannot be squeezed out. Which foundation is safer?
choices: Reward shipowners because they are fewer and richer.
Protect crew access because their demand can be satisfied without empowering equal rivals.
Avoid both sides and leave berths ungoverned.
questions.explanation: Shipowners want control that can become rivalry. Crews ask not to be oppressed, so public appeal hours can satisfy them without handing command to ambitious equals.

questions.prompt: Noble houses make a militia captain ruler during a tax revolt. Villagers expect punishment. What move helps him win the people?
choices: Keep extra levy tablets to prove loyalty to the noble houses.
Delay all tax decisions until the next quiet season.
Break the extra levy tablets and read a protection decree aloud.
questions.explanation: A noble-made ruler must seek the people if he began against them. Protection binds people more strongly when they expected harm.

questions.prompt: Before a siege scare, several nobles promise support. During the scare, some bind themselves to the prince's danger while others quietly open talks with the likely winner. How should the prince sort them?
choices: Treat all nobles alike because they are few.
Honor every noble who promised support in quiet times.
Distinguish bound allies, timid counselors, and ambitious nobles keeping a second door open.
questions.explanation: Quiet promises are weak evidence. Adversity reveals which nobles share the prince's fortune and which are thinking more of themselves than of him.

questions.prompt: A river prince calls for flood crews from the balcony, but citizens wait for the magistrates' drum. What has the flood revealed?
choices: His authority has not passed through the old magistrate channel.
The people hate flood defense in general.
Balcony orders are always useless in every city.
questions.explanation: The issue is not flood work or balcony style. Citizens still obey magistrates in tumults, so direct authority is weaker than quiet-time applause suggested.

questions.prompt: A dyer raised by guild workers receives a banquet offer from merchant houses. Workers still depend on wage courts and guard rotations for protection. What should he prioritize?
choices: Accept the banquet first because elite recognition makes workers loyal.
Close the wage court so no side feels favored.
Keep the wage measures and guard rotations working so people need the state and him daily.
questions.explanation: Popular support must become daily dependence, not ceremonial admiration. Merchant honors do not protect workers from domination tomorrow morning.

questions.prompt: A prince says, "The people praised me in quiet times, so adversity will prove their loyalty." What is missing from his reasoning?
choices: Quiet-time praise is enough if it happens in a large crowd.
He must ask whether people need the state and him when danger comes.
Adversity matters only for nobles, never for people.
questions.explanation: People promise freely when death is distant. The real test is whether their protection and daily order depend on the prince when the state needs them.

questions.prompt: A noble ally refuses to bind himself to the ruler's fortune, not from fear but because he is negotiating for his own rise. How should the ruler read him?
choices: As an ambitious danger to guard against like an open enemy.
As harmless because he has not openly rebelled.
As the safest counselor because he is independent.
questions.explanation: A timid noble can sometimes be used for counsel. An ambitious noble keeping himself free is preparing for his own advantage in adversity.

questions.prompt: A ruler raised by nobles wants security against a hostile people by rewarding the nobles with offices and exemptions. What is the problem?
choices: Nobles never matter in a civil principality.
The people are too many to secure against if hostile, while noble rewards may deepen oppression.
Offices and exemptions automatically make the people grateful.
questions.explanation: A prince can replace or manage some nobles, but he cannot secure himself against a hostile people. Noble privileges can worsen the very oppression people resist.

reviewCards.front: A leading citizen becomes prince without conquest or heredity. What origin question comes first?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the people or the nobles raised him. The source of favour tells you what demand now presses on the new ruler.

reviewCards.front: Nobles and people both support a ruler. Which demands differ?
reviewCards.back: Nobles often want to command and oppress. The people usually want not to be oppressed, a narrower demand that can be satisfied by protection.

reviewCards.front: A noble keeps a second door open before a siege. What should the ruler infer?
reviewCards.back: He is not bound to the ruler's fortune. If ambition drives the distance, he should be feared as someone ready to save himself by helping the expected winner.

reviewCards.front: Citizens applaud the prince but wait for magistrates in a flood. What failed?
reviewCards.back: Authority has not passed through the old channel. Direct rule is weak if people still receive real orders from magistrates in tumults.

reviewCards.front: Everyone promises loyalty in quiet times. What makes popular foundations real?
reviewCards.back: People must need the state and the prince in danger. Adversity tests whether protection and command have become practical dependence.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: When judging a civil ruler, begin with internal origin. Identify who raised the ruler, what that group wants, whether satisfying them would oppress others, and whether the people will need the ruler when danger arrives.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a leader rises through citizens rather than conquest, then name whether nobles or people elevated them before judging their security.
If powerful supporters ask for offices or exemptions, then test whether granting them would let equals oppress the people.
If crowds praise the ruler in calm times, then ask what daily protection makes them need the state and ruler when adversity comes.
If authority is moving from magistrates to direct command, then test who people obey during a real alarm, not during ceremony.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one leader raised by internal factions. Write four lines: who elevated them, what that group wants, how people are protected from oppression, and what adversity would test first.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, read one account of a leader raised by citizens and mark each noble ally as bound, timid but useful, or ambitious with a second door open.

memorableLines.text: The people can usually be satisfied by protection; nobles often want permission.
memorableLines.why: It gives the civil principality distinction in a compact contrast.

memorableLines.text: Quiet-time promises are not adversity loyalty.
memorableLines.why: It names the test that calm political support cannot pass by itself.

memorableLines.text: A prince built on the people is not standing on mud if he can command when danger arrives.
memorableLines.why: It corrects the easy proverb without turning popular support into a slogan.
